newsitem.title: GERMANY: German "summit" seeks ways out of jobs crisis.
newsitem.headline: German "summit" seeks ways out of jobs crisis.

text.p: Leading voices in the debate on how Germany should tackle its serious unemployment problems are due to speak out at an ambitious "jobs summit" in Berlin next week.

Trade union and business leaders, government and opposition politicians and even influential members of the clergy are due to attend a two-day conference organised by the German Trade Union Federation (DGB), which starts on Tuesday.
The opening of the conference will coincide with the release of March jobless data.
Unemployment figures rose to a post-war high over the winter and show no sign of a major turnaround in the German jobs market.
Billing the conference as a "forum for discussions", the DGB is nonetheless anxious that it should not be dismissed as merely an occasion for more rhetoric.
Union sources hinted on Friday that the conference could ultimately lead to a new thawing in the currently frosty relations between trade unions and Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government.

"Being indignant is not a tenable position forever," one said, referring to the unions' decision early last year to break off talks on job creation with Kohl after details of the government's current austerity package began to emerge.

In efforts to slim costs, the Kohl government pushed through a new law allowing companies to cut workers' pay to 80 percent during illness, a move which sparked furious demonstrations and prompted many companies to avoid following the law.

The protests, which rocked industries from metalworking to banking, marked the culmination of a worsening of industrial relations that followed the breakdown of a so-called "Alliance for Jobs" pact between unions, politicians and employers.
Under that alliance, unions said they were ready to trade low sector-wide wage increases for commitments to increase employment levels across the economy.

Informal talks have taken place in the last few months between Kohl and DGB chief Dieter Schulte, while union negotiators held closed meetings with employers on a reform of Germany's collective wage bargaining system.

But a more high-profile attempt to tackle the unemployment problem involving Kohl and the unions could help Kohl's profile, overshadowing recent criticism that he was not doing enough to tackle the problem.
On Thursday Kohl announced that he would stand for a fifth term in next autumn's federal elections and promised that he would not leave his work unfinished.
With 4.7 million out of work, Germany's so-called "social partners" are split along deep ideological grounds on what steps must be taken now.

Industry federations representing the main employers say that, with the domestic market increasingly open to rivals from abroad, wage bargaining and labour law is in general too inflexible to allow German firms to compete internationally.
They have argued for a relaxation of the legal framework surrounding work which would allow firms here the same freedom to "hire and fire" as their counterparts in the United States and Britain.

Trade unions and left-leaning politicans, meanwhile, plead in favour of a redistribution of work through a reduction in the millions of hours of overtime worked by Germans each year and schemes to allow earlier retirement.

Investment in areas such as training would allow Germany to extend its lead in productivity and manufacturing quality which have been largely responsible for its post-war economic success, they argue.

Unions have recently suggested that they would also be prepared to accept clauses in labour contracts allowing firms to reduce working hours during periods of slack demand -- but only if employers offer employment guarantees in return.

Apart from the heads of most of Germany's main trade unions, speakers at the Berlin summit are due to include Wolfgang Schaeuble, the powerful parliamentary leader of Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), and Rudolf Scharping, his opposite number in the rival SPD party.
Representatives of some of Germany's largest companies are also scheduled to address the conference, together with leaders of the Evangelical Church, one of the two main churches in Germany.
